edition: Issue 043: Kiwis raid their retirement at record pace, Dolly Parton's last song arrives with U2, and the Kiwis try to stop a haka from becoming a hug
tagline: Your 3-minute Saturday reset: a savings pot that keeps getting dipped into, a country legend signing off with Bono, and a rugby league final where the hardest job is keeping a cool head after the war dance.

stories.headline: Record 52,000 Kiwis raided their KiwiSaver in hardship - and good advice might have stopped them
stories.summary: More than 52,000 KiwiSaver members made hardship withdrawals in the year to June 2026, up from just over 20,000 in 2023, with total hardship withdrawals reaching $443.6 million in 2025 and now outpacing first-home withdrawals; a Victoria University report says many could have been avoided if people knew about other support.

body.text: KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals have hit record levels, and a new report says a decent chunk of them did not need to happen. More than 52,000 members made a hardship withdrawal in the year to June 2026 - up from just over 20,000 in 2023. Total hardship withdrawals have grown from $65 million in 2016 to $443.6 million in 2025, and Inland Revenue says withdrawals for genuine hardship now outpace withdrawals for first home deposits. The Victoria University report, led by law senior lecturer Victoria Stace and commissioned by the financial-capability charity FinCap, found many people who take the money out would not have done so had they been told about other support options first. It was flagged just as both major parties were campaigning on KiwiSaver changes - National proposed pushing contributions up to 12 percent and making them compulsory, Labour stopped short of making them compulsory for employees.

Who needs the promise of a golden retirement when you can raid the piggy bank for groceries right now? We are officially at the stage where New Zealanders are more likely to break into their own long-term savings than they are to get a first home deposit out of it - which is really saying something, given deposit maths now involves roughly a lifetime of winning lotto. The kicker, per the report, is that a lot of these withdrawals are like pressing the emergency button and then discovering the building has a fire escape, a ladder AND a kind firefighter - nobody told you the other help existed. And into this walks the election: both sides promised to make retirement savings bigger and compulsory, while the researchers quietly asked whether anybody had stopped to ask why people keep needing to claw it back out. Build a bigger pot if you like. Also, maybe mention the help that stops people needing to unstash it in the first place.

RNZ Business (13 Nov 2026, 'KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals hit record levels, but some could be avoided', Nine to Noon): more than 52,000 KiwiSaver members made hardship withdrawals in the 12 months to June 2026, up from just over 20,000 in 2023; total hardship withdrawals grew from $65 million (2016) to $443.6 million (2025); Inland Revenue reports hardship withdrawals now outpace first-home-deposit withdrawals; a Victoria University report led by Victoria Stace and commissioned by FinCap found many such withdrawals could have been avoided if savers knew about other support options; National proposed raising contributions to 12 percent and making contributions compulsory for employer and employee, while Labour's policy would not make employee contributions compulsory.

stories.headline: Dolly Parton's last song is out today - a tender U2 duet recorded three months before she died
stories.summary: 'Torn', Dolly Parton's final recording with U2, was released today as the closing track on Carnaval De Luz; Parton co-wrote it and recorded her vocal in Nashville in June, less than three months before her death on 25 August 2026 aged 80; Bono told the BBC the collaboration began when he bought her a set of bagpipes for her birthday.

body.text: Dolly Parton's final recording is out today. 'Torn', a duet with U2, closes Carnaval De Luz - U2's 16th studio album and first full-length since 2023. Parton co-wrote the track and recorded her vocal in Nashville, Tennessee, in June this year, less than three months before she died on 25 August 2026, aged 80, after a brief battle with cancer. When Bono recruited her for the duet, he did not realise it would be her swan song. 'We knew she was ill, but we had no idea that it'd be her last vocal,' he told the BBC. 'That was a real shock.' The collaboration began, reportedly, when Bono bought Parton a set of bagpipes for her birthday; she liked his demo work and offered him her own start on a song called Torn. Her original was about a woman choosing between two men; U2, with help from Jonny McDaid of Snow Patrol, rewrote it into a tale of a family divided by political differences. Two more versions of the track - from her longtime producer Kent Wells and T Bone Burnett - also dropped today.

Nobody loves a party trick more than learning that the entire backstory of Dolly Parton's very last song is 'Bono bought her some bagpipes.' We can picture the text back: lovely, thank you, here is a song, take it where you want. She wrapped up a whole legendary career with a bow while the biggest rock band on Earth was still faffing with the gift receipt. And in fairness to Dolly, she turned the polite small-talk of 'two men' into something about an entire family falling out over politics - country legend, and apparently the only person calm enough to make a U2 song understated. It is a farewell that lands somewhere between heartbreaking and unmistakably, gloriously Dolly: leave them a song they will argue about for years, and trust the world to remember you for the warmth, not the fight. Signing off with 'I've always loved you and always will' is a very hard note to follow. Somebody forward that to any politician who claims to have had the last word on anything, ever.

RNZ Music (13 Nov 2026, Al Newstead for RNZ, 'How U2 recruited Dolly Parton for posthumous duet'): 'Torn' is the closing track on Carnaval De Luz, U2's 16th studio album and first full-length since 2023; Parton co-wrote the track and recorded her vocal in Nashville in June 2026, less than three months before her death on 25 August 2026 aged 80 after a brief battle with cancer; Bono told the BBC they had no idea it would be her final vocal and called it 'a real shock'; the collaboration began when Bono bought Parton a set of bagpipes for her birthday; her original treatment concerned a woman choosing between two men, which U2 (with Jonny McDaid of Snow Patrol) rewrote into a story of a family divided by political differences; Kent Wells and T Bone Burnett each released their own versions of the track today.

stories.headline: Kiwis chase a first Rugby League World Cup title since 2008 - and the final's hardest ask is staying calm after the haka
stories.summary: New Zealand meet Australia in Sunday's Rugby League World Cup final at Allianz Stadium, hunting a first title since 2008; after Samoa were swept up in the emotion of their pre-match Sivi Tau and lost 44-12 in the semi, second-rower Isaiah Papali'i says the Kiwis must channel the haka's energy and 'turn on our footy brains'; Australia won the pool-stage thriller 24-22.

body.text: The Kiwis meet Australia at Allianz Stadium on Sunday in the Rugby League World Cup final, hunting their first title since 2008. The cautionary tale is fresh: in the semi-final, Samoa marched through their pre-match Sivi Tau and into the faces of the Australians - an imposing, emotional display - but once the whistle blew they slipped off early tackles, conceded two tries in the opening quarter and went down 44-12. Kiwis second-rower Isaiah Papali'i is confident his side can keep the haka's fire on the right side of the line. 'There's a lot of emotion in the haka, so we need to make sure that we reconnect, turn on our footy brains and use that emotion to our advantage rather than a hindrance,' he said. Fullback Kalyn Ponga, who says he stands at the back and lets the big boys lead during New Zealand's own war dance, is ready for another tense stare-down. The final is the second meeting of the tournament - Australia won the pool-stage thriller 24-22.

Only in rugby league do you hype a final by warning your own team: whatever you do, do NOT get too emotional before kick-off, because last week a fully-fired-up Samoa basically looked at Australia, got the butterflies, and went home. The most New Zealand sentence ever written about a World Cup final is a player saying the real challenge is to 'turn on our footy brains' - a man doing the world's most intimidating test of nerve and politely calling it a thinking exercise. Meanwhile Kalyn Ponga has already confirmed his job is to stand at the back and applaud the scary people doing the scary dancing. That is a man who knows his lane and stays in it. Australia, for their part, had to win an arm-wrestle in the pool stage and are probably thrilled to be facing a team this committed to emotional regulation. Fine. We will bring the cool heads AND the war dance. The Kangaroos can have the calm; we would just quite like the cup back after an 18-year nap.

RNZ Sport (13 Nov 2026, Jonty Dine, 'League: Kiwis know emotion must give way to execution in World Cup final'): the Kiwis meet Australia in Sunday's Rugby League World Cup final at Allianz Stadium, hunting a first title since 2008; Samoa lost the semi-final 44-12 after channelling huge emotion in their pre-match Sivi Tau but slipping off early tackles that led to two Australian tries; Kiwis second-rower Isaiah Papali'i said the side must 'reconnect, turn on our footy brains and use that emotion to our advantage rather than a hindrance'; fullback Kalyn Ponga said of the war-dance stare-down 'I just stand at the back and let the big boys lead'; Australia won the earlier pool-stage meeting 24-22.
